**Data:** \(T = 2\pi\ \text{s}\), \(v = b\sqrt{3}\ \text{m/s}\) at \(x = b\ \text{m}\), particle moving away from O.

**Step 1 — angular frequency.**
\(\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi}{2\pi} = 1\ \text{rad/s}\)

**Step 2 — amplitude.** For linear S.H.M., \(v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}\).

\(b\sqrt{3} = 1 \times \sqrt{A^2 - b^2}\)

Squaring: \(3b^2 = A^2 - b^2\), so \(A^2 = 4b^2\) and \(A = 2b\ \text{m}\).

**Step 3 — where the particle actually goes.** The particle is at \(x = b = \dfrac{A}{2}\) and is moving *away* from O, i.e. towards the extreme position at \(x = +2b\). That extreme lies a distance \(2b - b = b\) ahead of it. So a further distance \(b\) brings the particle **exactly to the extreme position** \(x = A = 2b\); it neither turns back nor retraces any part of its path, and the distance travelled equals the displacement.

**Step 4 — time.** Measuring time from the mean position, \(x = A\sin\omega t = 2b\sin t\).

At \(x = b\): \(\sin t_1 = \dfrac{b}{2b} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(t_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\ \text{s}\).

At \(x = 2b\): \(\sin t_2 = \dfrac{2b}{2b} = 1\), so \(t_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\ \text{s}\).

\(t = t_2 - t_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{3\pi - \pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\ \text{s}\)

\(\therefore\) the required time \(= \dfrac{\pi}{3} \approx 1.047\ \text{s}\).

**Check:** the journey is from phase \(\pi/6\) to phase \(\pi/2\), i.e. one-sixth of a full cycle, and \(\dfrac{T}{6} = \dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\ \text{s}\), which agrees.

For a body of mass \(m\) oscillating on a light spring of force constant \(k\), the period is \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\). The spring is the same in both cases, so \(k\) is unchanged.

**Case I** — mass \(m_1\) alone:

\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m_1}{k}}\) ... (1)

**Case II** — mass \(m_2\) tied to the first, so the oscillating mass is \((m_1 + m_2)\):

\(2T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m_1 + m_2}{k}}\) ... (2)

Dividing (2) by (1):

\(\dfrac{2T}{T} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_1 + m_2}{m_1}}\), i.e. \(2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_1 + m_2}{m_1}}\)

Squaring both sides:

\(4 = \dfrac{m_1 + m_2}{m_1}\)

\(4m_1 = m_1 + m_2\)

\(m_2 = 3m_1\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{m_1}{m_2} = \dfrac{1}{3}\), that is \(m_1 : m_2 = 1 : 3\).

The second body is three times as massive as the first.

**Given:** \(x = a\sin\omega t + b\cos\omega t\), where \(a\), \(b\) and \(\omega\) are constants.

**Part 1 — the motion is linear S.H.M.**

Differentiating with respect to time gives the velocity:

\(v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = a\omega\cos\omega t - b\omega\sin\omega t\)

Differentiating once more gives the acceleration:

\(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -a\omega^2\sin\omega t - b\omega^2\cos\omega t\)

\(\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -\omega^2\left(a\sin\omega t + b\cos\omega t\right)\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -\omega^2 x\)

Since \(\omega\) is a constant, \(\omega^2\) is a positive constant. Hence the acceleration of the particle is directly proportional to its displacement from the mean position and is directed opposite to that displacement, i.e. always towards the mean position. This is precisely the differential equation of linear S.H.M., so the particle performs linear S.H.M. of angular frequency \(\omega\) and period \(T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}\).

**Part 2 — the amplitude is \(A = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\).**

Because \(a\) and \(b\) are constants, we may always introduce two new constants \(A\ (>0)\) and \(\phi\) defined by

\(a = A\cos\phi\) and \(b = A\sin\phi\)

This substitution is always possible: squaring and adding,

\(a^2 + b^2 = A^2\cos^2\phi + A^2\sin^2\phi = A^2\left(\cos^2\phi + \sin^2\phi\right) = A^2\)

\(\therefore A = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\)

and dividing the two definitions fixes the angle, \(\tan\phi = \dfrac{b}{a}\).

Substituting back into the given displacement:

\(x = A\cos\phi\sin\omega t + A\sin\phi\cos\omega t\)

\(x = A\left(\sin\omega t\cos\phi + \cos\omega t\sin\phi\right)\)

Using \(\sin P\cos Q + \cos P\sin Q = \sin(P + Q)\),

\(x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)\)

This is the standard equation of a linear S.H.M. of amplitude \(A\), angular frequency \(\omega\) and epoch \(\phi\). Since \(\sin(\omega t + \phi)\) can range only between \(-1\) and \(+1\), the displacement lies between \(-A\) and \(+A\), so \(A\) is indeed the amplitude.

\(\therefore\) the particle performs a linear S.H.M. of amplitude \(A = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\), which is what was to be proved.

**Note:** the given motion is the superposition of two S.H.M.s of the same angular frequency \(\omega\), along the same line, with a phase difference of \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (one sine, one cosine) and amplitudes \(a\) and \(b\). The result \(A = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\) is the general amplitude formula \(A = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + 2ab\cos\delta}\) with \(\delta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so that \(\cos\delta = 0\).

**Data:** \(x_1 = 5\sin\left(4\pi t + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\ \text{cm}\), \(x_2 = 3\sin\left(4\pi t + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\ \text{cm}\)

So \(A_1 = 5\ \text{cm}\), \(\phi_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), \(A_2 = 3\ \text{cm}\), \(\phi_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

Both S.H.M.s are parallel and have the same angular frequency \(\omega = 4\pi\ \text{rad/s}\), so the resultant is also an S.H.M. of the same frequency.

**Phase difference:**

\(\delta = \phi_1 - \phi_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{4\pi - 3\pi}{12} = \dfrac{\pi}{12}\ \text{rad} = 15^\circ\)

**Resultant amplitude:**

\(R = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2A_1A_2\cos\delta}\)

\(R = \sqrt{(5)^2 + (3)^2 + 2(5)(3)\cos 15^\circ}\)

\(\cos 15^\circ = 0.9659\)

\(R = \sqrt{25 + 9 + 30 \times 0.9659} = \sqrt{34 + 28.98} = \sqrt{62.98}\)

\(\therefore R = 7.936 \approx 7.94\ \text{cm}\)

**Epoch (initial phase) of the resultant:**

\(\tan\phi = \dfrac{A_1\sin\phi_1 + A_2\sin\phi_2}{A_1\cos\phi_1 + A_2\cos\phi_2}\)

\(A_1\sin\phi_1 = 5\sin 60^\circ = 5 \times 0.8660 = 4.330\)

\(A_2\sin\phi_2 = 3\sin 45^\circ = 3 \times 0.7071 = 2.121\)

\(A_1\cos\phi_1 = 5\cos 60^\circ = 5 \times 0.5 = 2.500\)

\(A_2\cos\phi_2 = 3\cos 45^\circ = 3 \times 0.7071 = 2.121\)

\(\tan\phi = \dfrac{4.330 + 2.121}{2.500 + 2.121} = \dfrac{6.451}{4.621} = 1.396\)

\(\therefore \phi = 54^\circ 23' \approx 0.9492\ \text{rad}\)

**Result:** the resultant S.H.M. has amplitude \(R \approx 7.94\ \text{cm}\) and epoch \(\phi \approx 54^\circ 23'\), i.e.

\(x = 7.94\sin\left(4\pi t + 0.9492\right)\ \text{cm}\)

As expected, the epoch lies between the two component epochs \(45^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\), nearer the \(60^\circ\) one because that component has the larger amplitude.

**Data:** diameter \(D = 20\ \text{cm}\), so radius \(R = 0.1\ \text{m}\); \(M = 200\ \text{g} = 0.2\ \text{kg}\); \(\theta_{max} = 60^\circ\); \(T = 1\ \text{s}\); \(\pi^3 \approx 31\).

The disc hangs horizontally from the string and is twisted in its own plane, so it performs **angular S.H.M.** about the vertical string as axis. That axis passes through the centre of the disc and is perpendicular to its plane.

**Step 1 — moment of inertia of the disc.**

\(I = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.2 \times (0.1)^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.2 \times 0.01\)

\(I = 1 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{kg m}^2\)

**Step 2 — torsion constant of the string.** For angular S.H.M.,

\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{c}}\)

Squaring and rearranging,

\(c = \dfrac{4\pi^2 I}{T^2} = \dfrac{4\pi^2 \times 1 \times 10^{-3}}{(1)^2} = 4\pi^2 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{N m/rad}\)

**Step 3 — maximum restoring torque.** The restoring torque is \(\tau = -c\theta\), so it is greatest in magnitude at the extreme angular displacement \(\theta_{max}\).

\(\theta_{max} = 60^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\ \text{rad}\)

\(\tau_{max} = c\,\theta_{max} = 4\pi^2 \times 10^{-3} \times \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{4\pi^3}{3} \times 10^{-3}\ \text{N m}\)

Using the value given in the question, \(\pi^3 \approx 31\):

\(\tau_{max} = \dfrac{4 \times 31}{3} \times 10^{-3} = \dfrac{124}{3} \times 10^{-3} = 41.33 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{N m}\)

\(\therefore \tau_{max} \approx 4.13 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{N m}\)

That is, the maximum restoring torque generated in the string is about \(0.0413\ \text{N m}\).

**Data:** \(B = 1.6 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{Wb/m}^2\), \(I = 3 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{kg m}^2\), magnetic moment \(\mu = 3\ \text{A m}^2\).

A magnet vibrating in the plane of a uniform magnetic field performs angular S.H.M. with period

\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{\mu B}}\)

**Step 1 — the magnetic restoring couple per unit angular displacement.**

\(\mu B = 3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-5} = 4.8 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{N m/rad}\)

**Step 2 — period.**

\(\dfrac{I}{\mu B} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{-6}}{4.8 \times 10^{-5}} = 6.25 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{s}^2\)

\(\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{\mu B}} = \sqrt{6.25 \times 10^{-2}} = 0.25\ \text{s}\)

\(T = 2\pi \times 0.25 = \dfrac{\pi}{2} = 1.571\ \text{s}\)

**Step 3 — frequency and number of oscillations per minute.**

\(n = \dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{1}{1.571} = 0.6366\ \text{Hz}\)

Number of oscillations in one minute \(= 60n = \dfrac{60}{T} = \dfrac{60}{\pi/2} = \dfrac{120}{\pi}\)

\(= \dfrac{120}{3.142} = 38.20\)

\(\therefore\) the magnet performs about \(38\) oscillations per minute (period \(1.571\ \text{s}\), frequency \(0.6366\ \text{Hz}\)).

**Data:** amplitude \(A = 25\ \text{cm} = 0.25\ \text{m}\), \(g \approx \pi^2 \approx 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\).

**Step 1 — the condition for the block to stay in contact.**

Only two forces act on the block: its weight \(mg\) downwards and the normal reaction \(N\) of the piston upwards. Taking the upward direction as positive, the block's acceleration in S.H.M. is \(a = -\omega^2 x\), so Newton's second law gives

\(N - mg = ma = -m\omega^2 x\)

\(N = m\left(g - \omega^2 x\right)\)

The reaction is least when \(x\) is greatest and positive, i.e. at the **highest point** of the vibration, \(x = +A\):

\(N_{min} = m\left(g - \omega^2 A\right)\)

The block stays in contact only while \(N \geq 0\), therefore

\(\omega^2 A \leq g\), that is \(\omega \leq \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{A}}\)

(Physically: the piston must never accelerate downwards faster than a freely falling body, or it drops away from the block.)

**Step 2 — maximum frequency.** Taking \(g = \pi^2\ \text{m s}^{-2}\) as the question directs,

\(\omega_{max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{A}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\pi^2}{0.25}} = \sqrt{4\pi^2} = 2\pi\ \text{rad/s}\)

\(n_{max} = \dfrac{\omega_{max}}{2\pi} = \dfrac{2\pi}{2\pi} = 1\ \text{Hz}\)

\(\therefore\) the maximum possible frequency of vibration is \(1\ \text{Hz}\) (one oscillation per second).

**Step 3 — energy per unit mass at this frequency.** The total energy of a body of mass \(m\) performing S.H.M. is

\(E = \dfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2 A^2\)

\(\dfrac{E}{m} = \dfrac{1}{2}\omega^2 A^2\)

At the limiting frequency \(\omega^2 A = g\), so this simplifies neatly to

\(\dfrac{E}{m} = \dfrac{1}{2}gA = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 0.25\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{E}{m} = 1.25\ \text{J/kg}\)

(The same result follows directly: \(\dfrac{1}{2}(2\pi)^2(0.25)^2 = 0.125\pi^2\), which is \(1.25\ \text{J/kg}\) with \(\pi^2 \approx 10\).)
